unit_label: BRBL Module A unit 3: regulation of banking business

facts.statement: Power to issue directions (courseware): the Reserve Bank may issue directions to banks under Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949; those directions are binding on the bank or banks to which they are addressed even if not expressly described as statutory instructions. Section 21 gives power to regulate advances; Section 35A gives wide powers generally; the Reserve Bank has been issuing directions on rates of interest and other terms of acceptance of deposits and the making of loans and advances under Section 21 read with Section 35A. The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2017 inserted Sections 35AA and 35AB empowering the Reserve Bank to intervene directly in settling bad loan cases. Case law cited: the Gujarat High Court held that a Master Circular on wilful defaulters issued under statutory powers has the force of law even though it does not refer to a statute, and is not an impermissible delegation of legislative power; a non-statutory circular cannot create legal rights (State Bank of India v CIT); directions bind banks and not customers or the public; directions operate prospectively and a violation does not invalidate contracts with third parties (BOI Finance v Custodian); the power must be exercised in good faith (the supersession of a co-operative bank board upheld in the Harisidh co-operative bank case). Section 36(1)(a) allows the Reserve Bank to caution or prohibit banking companies against entering into any particular transaction or class of transactions and generally to give advice.

Acceptance of deposits (courseware): banks accept time and demand deposits from the public (fixed and recurring deposits are repayable after an agreed period, current and savings accounts are repayable on demand), subject to the terms and conditions agreed with the depositor and to Reserve Bank directions. Section 35A(c) lets the Reserve Bank give directions on acceptance of deposits in public interest, banking policy or depositor interest; at present the Reserve Bank prescribes only certain moratoria on acceptance of deposits, minimum and maximum period of deposits and the interest rates on NRI deposits, and clarifications on bulk deposits and KYC. Deposit insurance: deposits of banks including Regional Rural Banks and co-operative banks come within the Deposit Insurance and Credit Guarantee Corporation Act as amended in 2021, under which the bank pays an account holder up to the insured amount within 90 days if a bank comes under a moratorium. Returns on unclaimed deposits (Section 26): a bank must file a return every year within thirty days of the end of the calendar year of all deposits not operated for ten years (for fixed deposits, ten years from the expiry of the period of the deposit). The Banking Laws amendment of 2013 inserted Section 26A creating the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund to take over deposits not claimed or operated for ten years or more, within three months from the expiry of the ten years; the amount can be claimed back by the depositor or legal heirs or nominees at any time. Eligible accounts include savings, fixed or term deposits, cumulative or recurring deposits, current accounts, cash credit accounts, and balances of drafts, pay orders, bankers cheques and similar instruments.

Nomination (courseware): Section 45ZA of the Banking Regulation Act empowers a depositor or depositors of a banking company (which includes a co-operative bank) to nominate one person as nominee, in the prescribed manner, to whom the amount of the deposit will be returned on the death of the sole depositor or all depositors. The nominee must be the person entitled to all the rights of the depositor in the amount; the nomination can be varied or cancelled at any time by the depositor. Where the nominee is a minor, a person may be appointed to receive the amount on behalf of the minor. Payment to a nominee gives the bank a valid discharge, but does not affect the right of any claimant (such as a legal heir) against the nominee in respect of the amount received. Courts have held (Ram Chander Talwar v Devender Kumar Talwar) that nomination only ensures protection of the estate of the deceased until legal representatives take appropriate steps for succession. Rule 2 of the Banking Companies (Nomination) Rules, 1985 provides the procedure and forms for deposits; the Co-operative Banks (Nomination) Rules, 1985 provide similar rules. Articles in safe custody and safe deposit lockers: Sections 45ZC and 45ZE allow nomination of one person to receive the articles in the event of the death of the person who leaves articles in safe custody or hires a locker; the bank gets a valid discharge on return of the articles to the nominee, after an inventory in the prescribed manner for lockers. Banks must establish the identity of survivor or nominee and the fact of death with documentary evidence, find out whether any order from courts or forums restrains the bank from giving access, and make it clear that access is given only as a trustee of the legal heirs of the deceased hirer so that it does not affect the right or claim any person may have against the survivor or nominee. In a joint locker with survivorship clause, the mandate of the hirers is followed; similar procedure applies to articles in safe custody.

Loans and advances (courseware): lending is a core business of banks. Section 21 empowers the Reserve Bank to issue directions to control advances by banking companies generally or to any particular company, when satisfied that it is necessary in public interest, in the interests of depositors or in the interests of banking policy. Directions may cover: the purpose for which advances may or may not be made; margins to be maintained for secured advances; the maximum amount of advances or financial accommodation to any company, firm, association of persons or individuals, having regard to paid-up capital, reserves and deposits; the maximum amount of guarantees; and the rate of interest and other terms and conditions of advances. Selective credit control: the Reserve Bank may impose measures to prevent speculative hoarding of essential commodities (food grains, pulses, edible oils, sugar, jaggery, cotton and textiles) by regulating the quantum of credit and the rate at which it is extended; such measures have been little used in recent years. Restrictions on loans and advances (Section 20): a banking company cannot grant loans on the security of its own shares, and cannot enter into any commitment for granting loans or advances to or on behalf of any of its directors, or to firms in which any director is interested as partner, manager, employee or guarantor, or any company (other than a Section 25 / Section 8 company) in which a director holds substantial interest or is a director, managing agent, manager, employee or guarantor; loans to an individual whose guarantor or partner is a director are also barred. Where a transaction is doubtful as a loan or advance, the decision of the Reserve Bank is final. Section 20A: a banking company needs prior permission of the Reserve Bank to remit any debt to its directors or to a firm or company in which a director is interested; remission in contravention is void and of no effect.

Regulation of interest rates (courseware): the Reserve Bank regulates interest rates under Section 21 read with Section 35A. In regulating, there should be no discrimination against any class of depositors or loanees without justification in law (Harjit Singh v Union of India). Deposit interest rates were not regulated until 1964; later the Reserve Bank gave directions fixing deposit rates; interest rates on deposits and loans have been deregulated, subject to directions; savings deposit rates are regulated within the terms of the Reserve Bank Directions of 2016 as updated. Lending rates: advances interest is regulated under Section 21(2)(e) of the Act, but banks have freedom to decide lending rates, subject to directions on interest rates for weaker sections, exporters and small loans. The BPLR system (2003) was replaced by the Base Rate (1 July 2010), then the Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate (MCLR) from 1 April 2016 (comprising the marginal cost of funds, negative carry on account of CRR, operating costs and a tenor premium). The courseware then states that from 1 October 2019 all new floating rate personal or retail loans and floating rate loans to micro and small enterprises (and from 1 April 2020 to medium enterprises) must be linked to an external benchmark: the Reserve Bank repo rate, the three month or six month Treasury Bill yield published by the Financial Benchmarks India Pvt Ltd, or any other benchmark market interest rate published by it. Banks are free to choose the spread; credit risk premium may change only on a substantial change in the borrower credit assessment; the interest rate under an external benchmark shall be reset at least once in three months; the same bank may not adopt multiple benchmarks within a loan category. Usurious Loans Act, 1918 and Section 21A of the Banking Regulation Act: Section 21A provides that a transaction between a banking company and its debtor cannot be reopened by any court on the ground that the rate of interest charged is excessive; this overrides the Usurious Loans Act and other debt relief laws.

Internet banking (courseware): the Reserve Bank set up a Working Group on Internet banking that focused on technology and security, legal, and regulatory and supervisory issues. Highlights: banks should have a security policy approved by the Board; logical access controls (user ids, passwords, smart cards, biometrics); public key infrastructure should be the favoured technology; periodic penetration tests; physical access controls; backed-up data tested for recovery; disaster recovery sites; legal issues: accounts opened over the internet only after proper physical verification of identity; the Consumer Protection Act applies to banking services; regulatory issues: prior approval of the Reserve Bank for providing internet banking, reporting of breaches, only members of the cheque clearing system to participate in inter-bank payment gateways. The courseware adds that a November 2015 circular lays down the framework for internet banking facility for co-operative banks (view-only facility and transactional facility with prior approval and eligibility tests); general guidelines of 14 June 2001 and 5 November 2015 are referred to.

Money market instruments (courseware): the Reserve Bank of India (Amendment) Act, 2006 (Section 45W) empowers the Reserve Bank in public interest to regulate the financial system, to determine policy relating to interest rates or interest rate products and give directions to any agencies dealing in securities, money market instruments, foreign exchange, derivatives or instruments of like nature; the directions do not relate to the execution or settlement of trades on recognised stock exchanges. Call, notice and term money market: participants permitted include scheduled commercial banks (excluding local area banks), payment banks, small finance banks, regional rural banks, co-operative banks and primary dealers; prudential limits on borrowing are set as a percentage of capital funds or aggregate deposits (details dated and not taught). Certificates of deposit are issued by scheduled commercial banks, regional rural banks and small finance banks, in dematerialised form, held with a depository registered with SEBI, with a minimum denomination and tenor of seven days to one year, issued on a T+1 basis; banks may not grant loans against CDs; buyback only after a period. Commercial paper is a money market instrument under Section 45W issued under the Reserve Bank Commercial Paper Directions of 10 August 2017; eligible issuers include corporates, non-banking financial companies and all-India financial institutions meeting conditions; CP is issued in dematerialised form, as a promissory note at a discount to face value, with minimum credit rating A3, no underwriting or co-acceptance, and no options (call or put).

Banking Ombudsman and the Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (courseware): an Ombudsman is an independent non-partisan authority appointed to investigate public grievances and redress them as a non-adversarial alternative to courts. The Banking Ombudsman Scheme, 1995 was framed by the Reserve Bank under Section 35A, modified in 2002 and replaced by the Banking Ombudsman Scheme, 2006. The Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021 integrates the Banking Ombudsman Scheme, 2006, the Ombudsman Scheme for Non-Banking Financial Companies, 2018 and the Ombudsman Scheme for Digital Transactions, 2019, which were repealed; it is framed under Section 35A of the Banking Regulation Act, Section 45L of the RBI Act and Section 18 of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act and is focused on cost-free redress of complaints involving deficiency in service by regulated entities if not resolved to the satisfaction of the customer or not replied within 30 days by the regulated entity. Salient features: it is not necessary for a complainant to identify under which scheme to complain; deficiency in service is the ground, with a list of excluded grounds; the Scheme has done away with the jurisdiction of each ombudsman office; a Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre at the Reserve Bank in Chandigarh receives and processes complaints; the Principal Nodal Officer of the regulated entity, not below the rank of General Manager or equivalent, represents it; the regulated entity cannot appeal against an award if it did not furnish information in time; the Executive Director in charge of Consumer Education and Protection Department of the Reserve Bank is the Appellate Authority. The ombudsman must comply with Reserve Bank directions; the Scheme cannot override debt recovery tribunal jurisdiction, and where a complaint is under consideration by a court, tribunal or arbitrator the ombudsman cannot proceed (Durga Hotel Complex v Reserve Bank).

Financial stability and the reserve fund (courseware): financial stability has been defined by the Reserve Bank in its first Financial Stability Report (March 2010) as a situation in which the financial sector provides critical services to the real economy without discontinuity. Provisions in the Banking Regulation Act and the Reserve Bank Act promote stability through regulation of banks: reserve funds, cash reserve, statutory liquidity ratio and assets in India. Reserve fund (Section 17(1) of the Banking Regulation Act): every banking company incorporated in India must create a reserve fund; every year a sum equal to not less than twenty per cent of the profits as shown in the profit and loss account must be transferred to the reserve fund before any dividend is declared. The Reserve Bank instructed (circular of 23 September 2000) that commercial banks other than foreign banks must transfer not less than 25 per cent of net profit after tax from the year ending 31 March 2001, as stated in the courseware. Exemption: if a bank has adequate paid-up capital and reserves in relation to its deposit liabilities, the Reserve Bank may recommend to the Central Government exemption; no exemption is made unless the reserve fund together with the share premium account is not less than the paid-up capital. Appropriation from the reserve fund or share premium account must be reported to the Reserve Bank within twenty-one days. Foreign banks keep a deposit with the Reserve Bank of twenty per cent of annual profits of Indian business instead (Section 11(2)). Section 29A inserted by the 2013 amendment lets the Reserve Bank direct a bank to furnish statements and information on its business and affairs of associate enterprises.

Cash reserve (courseware): every scheduled bank has to maintain a cash reserve with the Reserve Bank under Section 42 of the Reserve Bank of India Act; in the case of non-scheduled banks, Section 18 of the Banking Regulation Act provides for the cash reserve. A scheduled bank is a bank included in the Second Schedule of the Reserve Bank Act; under Section 42(6) the Reserve Bank may include a bank if it has paid-up capital and reserves of an aggregate value of not less than Rs 5 lakh, satisfies the Reserve Bank that its affairs are not conducted detrimental to depositors, and is a State co-operative bank, a company as defined in Section 3 of the Companies Act, an institution notified by the Central Government, or a corporation or a company incorporated outside India (foreign bank). The Reserve Bank may exclude a bank if its paid-up capital and reserves fall below the limit or its affairs are conducted detrimentally to depositors or it goes into liquidation. Quantum (Section 42(1)): an average daily balance, as amended in 2006, of such per cent of the total of demand and time liabilities in India as the Reserve Bank notifies from time to time, having regard to the needs of securing monetary stability; the Reserve Bank can fix the ratio without any ceiling or floor rate (earlier floor three per cent and ceiling twenty per cent). Average daily balance is the average of the balances held at the close of business each day for the fortnight; the liabilities exclude paid-up capital, reserves and credit balance in the profit and loss account. Scheduled banks must maintain a minimum CRR balance of up to ninety per cent of the average daily required reserve on all days during the fortnight (courseware states 90 per cent). No interest is payable on CRR balances since the 2006 amendment. Returns: every scheduled bank submits a return, signed by two responsible officers, within seven days of the close of business on every alternate Friday, to the Reserve Bank (Section 42(2)); the Reserve Bank can allow provisional returns within seven days followed by final returns. Penalties: if the balance falls below the stipulated minimum, the bank is liable to penal interest at three per cent above the bank rate for the first fortnight and five per cent above the bank rate if the shortfall continues in the next fortnight; if the shortfall continues in the third fortnight each director, manager or secretary knowingly and wilfully party to the default is punishable with a fine; the Reserve Bank can also prohibit the bank from accepting fresh deposits. Penalty is payable within fourteen days of demand and the Reserve Bank may recover it as a decree of a civil court. Non-scheduled banks keep not less than three per cent of demand and time liabilities as at the last Friday of the second preceding fortnight, either in cash or as balance in current account with the Reserve Bank, and submit a monthly return by the twentieth day of the month.

Statutory liquidity ratio and assets in India (courseware): every banking company has to maintain a certain percentage of its net demand and time liabilities as liquid assets in India under Section 24 of the Banking Regulation Act, in the form and manner notified by the Reserve Bank. The Banking Regulation (Amendment) Ordinance, 2007 amended Section 24, removing the statutory floor of 25 per cent; under Section 24(2A) the scheduled bank in addition to the average daily balance of Section 42 of the RBI Act maintains assets valued at not less than such percentage as the Reserve Bank notifies, not exceeding 40 per cent of its total net demand and time liabilities on the last Friday of the second preceding fortnight. Non-scheduled banks maintain SLR assets in addition to the cash reserve under Section 18. Returns: a monthly return is submitted within twenty days after the month end showing the assets and liabilities at the close of business on every alternate Friday. Penalty for default: penal interest at three per cent above the bank rate on the shortfall, rising to five per cent above the bank rate if the default continues on the succeeding alternate Friday; directors, managers and secretaries of the bank are punishable with a fine on continued default; the Reserve Bank may waive the penalty when it is satisfied that the bank had sufficient reason. Assets in India (Section 25): the assets in India of every banking company at the close of business on the last Friday of every quarter shall not be less than 75 per cent of its demand and time liabilities in India; the bank submits a return within one month from the end of every quarter; regional rural banks submit the report to NABARD. Assets include cash, gold or unencumbered approved securities, and export bills drawn in India and import bills drawn on and payable in India approved by the Reserve Bank; paid-up capital, reserves and credit balance in the profit and loss account are not liabilities in India for this purpose.

payload.title: The power of the Reserve Bank to issue directions
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Sections 21 and 35A** let the Reserve Bank give **directions to banks**. Directions are **binding on the banks addressed** even if not labelled statutory.

- **Section 21**: regulation of **advances**; **Section 35A**: **wide general powers**, including directions on deposit interest and lending.
- **2017 amendment**: **Sections 35AA and 35AB** let the Reserve Bank direct action on **bad loans**.
- **Case law (as the courseware cites it):** a **Master Circular under statutory power has the force of law**; a **non-statutory circular creates no legal rights**; directions bind **banks, not customers or the public**; they apply **prospectively** and do not void **contracts with third parties**; the power must be used in **good faith**.
- **Section 36(1)(a)**: the Reserve Bank may **caution or prohibit** banks against particular transactions and **give advice**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Directions are a quicker regulatory tool than amending the Act, but only those backed by statutory power carry the force of law.

self_check.prompt_text: Which sections give the Reserve Bank the power to issue binding directions to banks?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Sections 21 and 35A of the Banking Regulation Act.

payload.title: Acceptance of deposits and unclaimed deposits
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Types:** **time deposits** (fixed, recurring) are repayable after the agreed period; **demand deposits** (current, savings) on demand, under the agreed terms and **Reserve Bank directions**.

**Directions under Section 35A(c)** can cover **moratoria**, **minimum and maximum periods**, **NRI deposit rates**, bulk deposit and **KYC** matters.

**Deposit insurance:** under the **DICGC Act (as amended in 2021)** the account holder is paid up to the insured amount within **90 days** of a bank moratorium (the amount is not taught here as it is dated).

**Unclaimed deposits:**

- **Section 26:** annual **return within 30 days of the end of the calendar year** of all deposits **not operated for ten years** (for fixed deposits, ten years from the **expiry of the deposit period**).
- **Section 26A (2013):** deposits unclaimed for **ten years or more** pass to the **Depositor Education and Awareness Fund** within **three months**; the depositor, legal heirs or nominee **can claim them back at any time**.
- **Eligible accounts:** savings, fixed or term, recurring, current, cash credit credit balances, and balances of **drafts, pay orders and bankers cheques**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The Fund keeps unclaimed money usable by the depositor while the bank no longer treats it as its own liability.

self_check.prompt_text: After how many years of inactivity is a deposit transferred to the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund?

payload.title: Nomination for deposits, safe custody and lockers
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Deposits (Section 45ZA):** a depositor may **nominate one person** to receive the deposit on the **death of the sole depositor or all depositors**; the nomination can be **varied or cancelled** at any time. For a **minor nominee**, a person may be **appointed to receive the money** on the minor's behalf.

**Effect:** payment to the nominee gives the bank a **valid discharge**, but a **legal heir's rights against the nominee remain** (the courts treat the nominee as holding for the heirs).

**Rules:** the **Banking Companies (Nomination) Rules, 1985** and **Co-operative Banks (Nomination) Rules, 1985**.

**Safe custody and lockers (Sections 45ZC and 45ZE):** one person may be nominated to receive the **articles** or **locker contents** after the hirer's death, after an **inventory**. Before access the bank must **verify identity and death**, **check for court orders** restraining access, and **tell the survivor or nominee** that access is **as trustee for the legal heirs**. Joint lockers follow the **survivorship clause** (either or survivor, anyone or survivor).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Nomination is a quick way to pay the bank safely, not a way to override succession law.

self_check.prompt_text: Does payment to a nominee defeat the claims of the legal heirs of the deceased depositor?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No. The bank gets a valid discharge but the legal heirs may still claim against the nominee.

payload.title: Loans and advances: Section 21 directions and the Section 20 limits
payload.expanded_explanation_md: These limits stop a bank from becoming a private source of credit for its own directors.

self_check.prompt_text: Whose permission is needed to remit a debt owed by a director of the bank?

payload.title: Interest rate regulation, MCLR and external benchmark lending
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Power:** Section **21 read with Section 35A**; the Reserve Bank must **not discriminate** among classes of depositors or borrowers without legal justification.

**Deregulation:** deposit rates were not regulated until **1964**; both **deposit and lending rates are now largely free** (with exceptions for **weaker sections, exporters and small loans**).

**Benchmarks:** **BPLR (2003)** gave way to the **Base Rate (1 July 2010)**, then **MCLR (1 April 2016)**: **marginal cost of funds + negative carry on CRR + operating costs + tenor premium**. MCLR reflects the **current marginal cost**, while the Base Rate reflected the **average cost**.

**External benchmark (the courseware's 2019-20 rule):** new **floating rate retail and MSE loans** are linked to the **repo rate**, the **3-month or 6-month Treasury Bill yield** published by FBIL, or another published benchmark; **banks choose the spread**; the **credit risk premium** may change only on **substantial change in credit assessment**; the rate is **reset at least once every three months**; **one benchmark per loan category** in a bank.

**Section 21A:** a court cannot **reopen a bank transaction because the rate is excessive**; it overrides the **Usurious Loans Act, 1918**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Linking loan rates to an external benchmark makes policy rate changes pass through to borrowers faster.

self_check.prompt_text: How often must the interest rate under an external benchmark be reset at the latest?
self_check.expected_takeaway: At least once in three months.

payload.title: Internet banking guidelines
payload.core_explanation_md:
The Reserve Bank's Working Group looked at **technology and security**, **legal** and **regulatory and supervisory** aspects.

- **Technology:** a **Board-approved security policy**, **logical access controls** (user ids, passwords, smart cards, biometrics), **public key infrastructure** as the favoured technology, **periodic penetration tests**, **physical access controls**, **tested backups** and **disaster recovery sites**.
- **Legal:** accounts opened over the internet only after **physical verification of identity**; the **Consumer Protection Act** applies to banking services.
- **Regulatory:** **prior Reserve Bank approval** to offer internet banking; **report breaches**; only **members of the cheque clearing system** take part in inter-bank payment gateways.

The courseware also mentions the **2015 circular** for co-operative banks (**view-only** and **transactional** facilities).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Security rules matter more here than in branch banking because the customer is not physically present.

self_check.prompt_text: Whose prior approval does a bank need to provide internet banking?

payload.title: Regulation of money market instruments
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Section 45W** (RBI Act, **Amendment Act 2006**) lets the Reserve Bank regulate **interest rate products** and **money market instruments, foreign exchange and derivatives** in public interest; it does **not** extend to **trades on recognised stock exchanges**.

- **Call, notice and term money:** participants include **scheduled commercial banks, payment banks, small finance banks, RRBs, co-operative banks and primary dealers**; **prudential borrowing limits** apply (dated figures not taught).
- **Certificates of deposit:** issued by **scheduled commercial banks, RRBs and small finance banks** in **dematerialised form**; **no loans against CDs**.
- **Commercial paper:** a **money market instrument** under **Section 45W**; issued as a **promissory note at a discount**, in **dematerialised form**, **minimum rating A3**, **no underwriting or co-acceptance**, **no call or put options**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: These instruments are short term and mostly wholesale, which is why the Reserve Bank directs rather than legislates for them.

self_check.prompt_text: Under which section is commercial paper treated as a money market instrument regulated by the Reserve Bank?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Section 45W of the Reserve Bank of India Act.

payload.title: The Banking Ombudsman and the Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021
payload.core_explanation_md:
An **Ombudsman** is an **independent, non-partisan** authority that handles public grievances as an **alternative to court**.

**History:** **Banking Ombudsman Scheme 1995** under **Section 35A** (modified 2002; **2006 Scheme**). The **Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021** merged the **Banking Ombudsman Scheme 2006**, the **Ombudsman Scheme for NBFCs 2018** and the **Ombudsman Scheme for Digital Transactions 2019**, which were **repealed**.

**Integrated Scheme features:** complaint if the entity **did not reply within 30 days** or the customer is **dissatisfied**; **deficiency in service** is the ground, with listed **exclusions**; the complainant need **not name the scheme**; **no territorial jurisdiction per office**; a **Centralised Receipt and Processing Centre at Chandigarh**; the regulated entity appoints a **Principal Nodal Officer** not below **General Manager rank**; an entity **cannot appeal** if it did not give **timely information**; the **Executive Director in charge of Consumer Education and Protection Department** is the **Appellate Authority**.

The ombudsman **follows Reserve Bank directions** and does **not proceed** on a matter taken to **court, tribunal or arbitration**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Merging three schemes meant a customer no longer needed to know which scheme covered the regulated entity.

self_check.prompt_text: Within how many days of the entity not replying may a customer approach the ombudsman under the Integrated Scheme?
self_check.expected_takeaway: After thirty days with no reply or an unsatisfactory reply.

payload.title: Financial stability and the reserve fund (Section 17)
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Financial stability** (Reserve Bank): a situation where the financial sector provides **critical services to the real economy without discontinuity**.

**Provisions that promote it:** the **reserve fund**, **cash reserve**, **statutory liquidity ratio** and **assets in India**.

**Reserve fund (Section 17(1)):** every banking company incorporated in India transfers **not less than 20 per cent of its profit** (per the profit and loss account) to the reserve fund **before declaring any dividend**. The courseware adds that the **Reserve Bank instructed 25 per cent** of net profit after tax for commercial banks (other than foreign banks) from the year ended **31 March 2001** (flagged as unverified).

- **Exemption:** the Government may exempt on the Reserve Bank's recommendation if capital and reserves are adequate against deposits, but not unless the **reserve fund plus share premium account is at least the paid-up capital**.
- **Appropriation** from the fund must be **reported within 21 days**.
- **Foreign banks** do not create the fund; they **deposit 20 per cent of annual Indian profit** with the Reserve Bank (**Section 11(2)**).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Retained reserves build a cushion that lets the bank absorb losses before they hit depositors.

self_check.prompt_text: What minimum share of profit must a banking company transfer to the reserve fund under Section 17(1)?

payload.title: Cash reserve (CRR) under Section 42 of the RBI Act
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Who:** every **scheduled bank** keeps a cash reserve with the Reserve Bank (**Section 42**); **non-scheduled banks** under **Section 18 of the BR Act**.

**Scheduled bank (Second Schedule):** the Reserve Bank may include a bank that has **paid-up capital and reserves of at least Rs 5 lakh**, whose affairs are **not detrimental to depositors**, and that is a **State co-operative bank, a company, a notified institution or a foreign company**; it may **exclude** a bank that falls below Rs 5 lakh, is run detrimentally or goes into **liquidation**.

**Quantum (Section 42(1), 2006 amendment):** an **average daily balance** of a **percentage of demand and time liabilities in India** notified by the Reserve Bank, with **no floor or ceiling** in the Act. **No interest** is paid on CRR balances. The courseware states that a **minimum of 90 per cent** of the required balance must be kept **every day** of the fortnight.

**Returns:** a **signed return by two officers**, within **seven days** of every **alternate Friday**.

**Penalty:** **3 per cent above the bank rate** on the shortfall in the **first fortnight** and **5 per cent above** if it **continues**; further default makes **directors, managers or secretaries** liable to a **fine**; the Reserve Bank may **bar fresh deposits**; the penalty is due within **14 days** of demand.

**Non-scheduled banks:** at least **3 per cent** of demand and time liabilities, in cash or a **current account with the Reserve Bank**, with a **monthly return** by the **20th**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The CRR gives the Reserve Bank a lever over money supply and a guaranteed pool of liquidity held at the central bank.

self_check.prompt_text: What penal rate applies to a first-fortnight CRR shortfall?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Three per cent above the bank rate.

payload.title: Statutory liquidity ratio and assets in India
payload.core_explanation_md:
**SLR (Section 24 of the BR Act):** every bank holds a **percentage of net demand and time liabilities** as **liquid assets in India**, in the form notified by the Reserve Bank. After the **2007 Ordinance** the Act has **no 25 per cent floor**; the Reserve Bank can set the ratio **up to 40 per cent** of net demand and time liabilities. **Non-scheduled banks** hold SLR assets **in addition to their Section 18 cash reserve**.

**Returns:** a **monthly return within 20 days** of the month end, with positions on **every alternate Friday**.

**Penalty:** **3 per cent above the bank rate** on a shortfall, rising to **5 per cent above** if it continues; **directors, managers and secretaries** are liable to a **fine** on continued default; the Reserve Bank may **waive** it where there was **sufficient reason**.

**Assets in India (Section 25):** on the **last Friday of every quarter**, assets in India must be at least **75 per cent of demand and time liabilities in India**; the return is due **within a month of the quarter end** (RRBs report to **NABARD**). Assets include **cash, gold, unencumbered approved securities** and approved **export and import bills**; **paid-up capital, reserves and credit balance in the profit and loss account** are **not liabilities in India**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: SLR and the assets in India rule together keep banking funds invested in safe, liquid assets inside the country.

self_check.prompt_text: What share of demand and time liabilities in India must be held as assets in India?
self_check.expected_takeaway: At least 75 per cent, at the close of the last Friday of every quarter.

payload.stem_md: The Reserve Bank issues directions on advances and deposits to banks mainly under

The Ordinance removed only the statutory floor; the SLR requirement itself continues.

options.text_md: Removing the statutory minimum of 25 per cent for the SLR
options.explanation_md: The courseware says the floor was removed.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The 2007 change removed the floor.

payload.stem_md: Under Section 25, the assets in India of a banking company on the last Friday of a quarter must not be less than

options.text_md: Seventy-five per cent of its demand and time liabilities in India
options.explanation_md: The Act sets seventy-five per cent.
Forty per cent is the SLR ceiling.
Twenty per cent is the reserve fund transfer.
No such requirement.

payload.correct_explanation_md: The assets in India test is seventy-five per cent.

payload.stem_md: Which of these is treated as an asset in India for Section 25?

options.explanation_md: Paid-up capital is not a liability in India or asset.

options.text_md: Export bills drawn in India approved by the Reserve Bank
options.explanation_md: The courseware includes approved export and import bills.

options.text_md: Assets held with the head office abroad
options.explanation_md: Assets must be in India.
Only unencumbered approved securities count.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Approved bills and unencumbered securities qualify.

payload.stem_md: For the assets in India return, regional rural banks submit the report to

options.explanation_md: SEBI does not receive the return.
The Registrar does not receive it.
The courseware states RRBs report to NABARD.
The report goes to NABARD.

payload.correct_explanation_md: RRBs report to NABARD.

payload.stem_md: A bank has demand and time liabilities in India of Rs 800 crore at the close of the last Friday of a quarter. What is the minimum value of assets in India it must hold, in crore rupees, under Section 25?
payload.correct_explanation_md: 75 per cent of Rs 800 crore = Rs 600 crore.

payload.stem_md: The bank rate is 6.25 per cent. A scheduled bank has a CRR shortfall in the first fortnight. What is the annual penal interest rate, in per cent?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the rate in per cent.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Penal rate = 6.25 + 3 = 9.25 per cent.

payload.stem_md: With the same bank rate of 6.25 per cent, the shortfall continues into the next fortnight. What is the annual penal interest rate, in per cent?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the rate in per cent.

payload.correct_explanation_md: Penal rate = 6.25 + 5 = 11.25 per cent.

payload.stem_md: A bank has a CRR shortfall of Rs 365 crore for one day. The penal interest is 9.5 per cent a year on a 365 day basis. What is the penal interest for the day, in lakh rupees?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the amount in lakh rupees (1 crore = 100 lakh).

payload.correct_explanation_md: Interest = 365 crore x 9.5 per cent / 365 = Rs 0.095 crore = Rs 9.5 lakh.

payload.stem_md: A bank has a profit of Rs 250 crore shown in the profit and loss account. What is the minimum transfer to the reserve fund at the statutory twenty per cent, in crore rupees?
payload.correct_explanation_md: 20 per cent of Rs 250 crore = Rs 50 crore.

payload.stem_md: A non-scheduled bank has demand and time liabilities of Rs 2,000 crore on the last Friday of the second preceding fortnight. What is the minimum cash reserve at three per cent, in crore rupees?
payload.correct_explanation_md: 3 per cent of Rs 2,000 crore = Rs 60 crore.

payload.stem_md: A bank has net demand and time liabilities of Rs 1,500 crore. If the Reserve Bank sets the SLR at the statutory ceiling of forty per cent, how much must the bank hold as SLR assets, in crore rupees?
payload.correct_explanation_md: 40 per cent of Rs 1,500 crore = Rs 600 crore.

payload.stem_md: A fixed deposit matured in 2013 and was not claimed. Counting ten years from expiry of the deposit period, in which year does it become eligible for return of unclaimed deposits under Section 26?

numeric_rule.rounding_instruction: Give the year as a whole number.

unresolved: The unit is the courseware account of Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and RBI Act, 1934 provisions (Sections 17, 20, 20A, 21, 21A, 24, 25, 26, 26A, 35A, 35AA, 36, 45ZA, 45ZC, 45ZE) and of Reserve Bank directions. No Act text and no Reserve Bank direction was retrieved, so section numbers and rules are taught only as the courseware states them and must be checked against the Acts and current directions at the 30 June 2026 cut-off (the Banking Laws (Amendment) Act, 2025 changed nomination rules, among others) before publication.

Held back as dated or likely superseded and not asked in any question: the MCLR methodology as a current benchmark detail (the courseware states external benchmark lending applies to new floating rate retail and MSE loans from 1 October 2019 and to medium enterprises from 1 April 2020; only the principle is taught), interest rate on the unclaimed deposits transferred to the Depositor Education and Awareness Fund (4, 3.5 and 3 per cent dated steps), the Rs 5 lakh deposit insurance limit and 90 day payout rule, minimum denominations, tenors and eligibility conditions for certificates of deposit and commercial paper, call and notice money prudential limits, the 2015 internet banking circular details including the cooperative bank eligibility thresholds, the 2020 and 2021 CRR exemptions for incremental lending, and the list of items credited to the Fund.

The cash reserve ratio is taught only as the statutory structure: a scheduled bank keeps an average daily balance fixed by the Reserve Bank (no floor or ceiling since the 2006 amendment) and the courseware states a daily minimum of 90 per cent of the required balance; the present ratio and the statutory liquidity ratio level (the Act caps it at 40 per cent) are not taught as current.

The courseware text on the old Banking Ombudsman Scheme (one month, 15 days acceptance and extension) is repealed by the Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021 and is not taught; the Scheme itself is covered fully in a later unit and only its outline is taught here.

The statement that the reserve fund transfer is 20 per cent under the Act and 25 per cent by Reserve Bank instruction from 2001 is a courseware statement; the 25 per cent figure is flagged as unverified and is taught as the courseware states it, with the statutory 20 per cent separately.
